utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, first --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before Mr. Stein starts, I understand from something that the Victims and Witnesses Unit has told us that the witness may have something that he wants to raise with the Tribunal. We had the message indirectly from the people who accompanied the witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Doctor, is there something you want to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wonder if I might be permitted about five minutes to clarify responses that I gave to a line of questioning yesterday in regard to the one man, one vote matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. If you will recall, yesterday, I was asked a series of questions by Mr. Stein dealing with a quotation from the book Yugoslavia: Death of a Nation by Laura Silber and Allan Little, specifically a quote which referred to one man, one vote in the relationships between President Izetbegovic and the HDZ. Mr. Stein also then, in response to an inquiry from you, stated that this was the big debate about the status of the Croatian community. I believe it was not the big debate or, in fact, any debate at all, and I did not have in front of me yesterday the context from the work of Silber and Little, which shows, I think quite clearly, the nature of this issue and the fact that it was very short-lived and inconsequential. I can use the ELMO, sir, if you wish, or I can just read, but it's about ten sentences from the book and a bit of explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may help if you put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Dr. Donia read slowly, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Ma'am. Beginning here on page 209 was the question that was stated to me yesterday. "Like the Serbs, the Croats were infuriated when Izetbegovic announced in September that the SDA opposed the principle of national parity, and that the next government would be formed on the basis of one-man one-vote." I believe this statement to be completely accurate, but there's an important qualification that must be added, namely, the meaning of the word "government." In the structure at the time, the government was a specific institution. It was independent of the assembly and independent of the presidency. It was, in fact, a body called the government or vlada which was a group of -- there was a president of it and vice-presidents and the various ministers. So Izetbegovic's proposal did not pertain to voting in the assembly, did not pertain to membership on the presidency, which was already decided in the constitution, but only to the composition of the government. So this statement is, I believe, factually correct. However, the speculation that follows on the part of the authors assumes that it pertains to all governmental institutions, and it sets off this following speculative conclusion: "Izetbegovic was attempting to play the same game in Bosnia that Milosevic had in mind for Yugoslavia." Now, that's only true to a very limited degree because what Milosevic had in mind for Yugoslavia was, in fact, a national voting for an assembly, which was one man, one vote. "Unless civil and individual rights were secured through institutions, majority vote would guarantee Serb domination throughout the country." Now, the institutions that the author is assuming here are all institutions, and I would point out at the time that civil and individual rights were already secured by a variety of institutions. In force, perhaps not, but secured. The authors then go on: "In Bosnia, the same principle would give the Muslims, the Republic's largest ethnic group with 44 per cent of the 4,35 million population, the greatest authority." This was true already. There was no change in the situation from the last days of socialism to the time that this statement pertains to. Then a very speculative conclusion: "A key difference was that Milosevic was striving for changes which subverted the very principles on which Yugoslavia was founded, whereas Izetbegovic's proposals applied only to Bosnia." The final statement of this paragraph: "The Republic's constitution, however, made each of its three groups constituent nations which meant that no major decision could be carried out without consensus." As a matter of fact, the first part of that sentence is absolutely correct. Each of the Serbs, Croats, and Muslims were recognised as constituent nations. The latter part of that sentence is not the case. It is not true that no major decision could be carried out without consensus. This is a very important issue because the constitution in effect at the time defined national communities but gave them no veto power over decision-making, either in the assembly nor in the presidency. In fact, there are numerous examples, both before the election of November 18th, 1990 and after the election, in which decisions were made by those two bodies with the complete opposition of one of the constituent nations. In other words, the status quo was that constituent nations could not obstruct a decision. There was no requirement for consensus. Now, the key part of this, however, is it's still true that the Croats and Serbs were infuriated with Izetbegovic in September. Unfortunately, yesterday, Mr. Stein didn't go on to point out the subsequent sentence at the top of page 210: "Despite the growing tensions, the three national parties, meeting behind closed doors in Sarajevo, agreed to form a united front against their main opponents, the communists." This agreement, which I will represent to you took place in October 1990, prior to the elections, resolved the issue of one man, one vote for all three major parties. It was replaced with a notion that to include the government itself, that council of ministers and various ministry positions, would be generally guided by the census of 1990. I must represent this to you. I don't have with me the documentation to establish this, but I am confident you will have other opportunities to affirm this point. From the time of this agreement onward to today, this issue of one man, one vote, ceased to be a point of contention between the parties. I've just finished six weeks of going through the daily press in Sarajevo from November 1990 until April of 1992, this was in research for another matter, and I never saw a single reference to a debate about one man, one vote versus recognition of communities. There was, however, a very important overriding debate that seized the HDZ, and it was not the one man, one vote issue; it was the question of whether the HDZ would be a party representing all Croats in Bosnia, that is, the national community, or whether it would become a territorial entity defined by the boundaries of Herceg-Bosna as spelled out in November 1991, ruled under what was essentially a constitutionally conditioned martial law as proclaimed on July 3, 1992, and under the fused leadership of the HVO, the HDZ, and the Community of Herceg-Bosna, all responsive to the instructions of President Izetbegovic. Now, that polarity between those people who wanted the HDZ to represent all Croats and those who favoured a territorial unit which excluded about 250.000 Croats from representation, that controversy was ultimately decided because of the Zagreb regime's involvement in favour of the territorial option and leads us to the background of the events discussed in the indictment. I find no evidence of further discussion of one man, one vote, after this September reference that's in the book. I would also just like to point out that the quotations that were given to me yesterday from the book were highly selective, were taken out of context, and omitted some key things which this author, on the very same page, has said about topics that were part of my direct testimony. At the bottom of page 208, you see the point made by the two authors, "National Dreams: The Emergence of Ethnic Parties and Leaders," did not reflect ancient hatreds, as was later claimed by some sectors of the frustrated international community while it struggled to comprehend the war." That was not something that was shown to you yesterday. Nor were the comments that the authors have to make about Dario Kordic shown to you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think we're now going beyond what's necessary for the moment. No doubt, if we refer to the book, we can look at it in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, just one or two brief administrative things. We have substituted for the illegible copies of D42 some new copies. I hope they work; if not, we'll try again. With an opportunity, Judge, I would like to address the issue of the tape that we addressed at the end of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: After the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, let me start by asking you this, and that is, did you have the Silber book with you when you came to The Hague today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never leave home without it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Never leave home without it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had it with me when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm listening by the way, Judge, to French, so when the French ends, I will begin, and I hope to avoid any speed warnings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So it's kind of like an American Express card: You never leave home without it because it's important?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You don't consider yourself an advocate for one side of this case versus another, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't consider myself an advocate, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let's take one brief look at what you said yesterday relative to some quotes from Mr. Izetbegovic that I gave you. I don't want to repeat them. It's the only thing of your testimony yesterday I want to go over. It was relative to the quotes in which he essentially said, "In our state, we will live how it suits us. No one can prescribe how we should live," et cetera. You were asked when he said that and were you familiar with it, and your response was, quote, "I think it comes from the Islamic declaration written by Mr. Izetbegovic." In fact, sir, I represent to you that that is from a 1994 speech given in May in Mecca, and this of course would be just after the Washington Accords.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I request, sir, to see that document? You've given me many quotes in the last -- yesterday that you've represented as coming from various places, and I would really like to see the exact quote that you're operating from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I have no problem with that. We'll show you the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does it matter? What does it matter which was the date of the quotation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The question then, sir, as per the Presiding Judge's query, is, this was in 1994; doesn't that give us a different insight, as of 1994, as to what the leader of the Bosnian Muslims was advocating as of that time period?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Stein, in order to clarify what has been said by the witness, I think that we should have precise indications as to the context of this speech that you said was given in May in Mecca. (In English) Given in what context, on what occasion? This is very important. Was it an official speech or a personal interview? What was it, exactly? This is important, to know what we are talking about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Judge, according to the text we have, this was a speech given by Mr. Izetbegovic, addressing pilgrims and Bosniak heroes, delivered in Mecca publicly in 1994, May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the witness would like to see where you get that information from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Where was it published?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: This is our only copy, but certainly you may see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Where was it published?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In 1975. I'm sorry; 1995, and it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Where? Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Which paper was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: According to the title page, it was published by the Muslim Community in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And the quote has a Post-It on the beginning and is highlighted for you in yellow next.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What you've showed me, sir, is not a speech; it's an interview with a publication, Ljiljan, a Sarajevo newspaper, dated December 10th, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You're looking at the wrong Post-It, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: While the witness is reviewing the document, we have for the Court four copies, if you would like, and we can put it into evidence. This is a copy not of the entire book but of the specific speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, I hope we're not going to go over all the evidence of yesterday again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I wasn't planning to, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Very well. You can put that in, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. Did you wish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Put it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. I think we're shy one copy for my adversaries, but we'll make sure that's remedied.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D44/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Dr. Donja, are you ready to resume your examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, can we turn our attentions from the document in front of you to an issue involving the 1990 elections? You and I can agree that the 1990 elections transformed the political landscape in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And indeed, you've noted that the elections demonstrated the remarkable historical consistency with previous Bosnian multi-party elections from 1910 and 1920?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And each of the ethnic groups essentially voted for their ethnic party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In substantial percentages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And your observation at that time was: "The politicians restored patterns of coalition politics in the Bosnian assembly in a futile effort to achieve a formula for Bosnia's political future that would satisfy all parties."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I made no comment in writing on the elections in 1990 at the time, so I'm wondering where you're reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, I'm reading from your book, at page 211, and specifically quoting from it, sir, the last --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll agree that that's from my book, but it was not written in 1990, as you suggest in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sorry, your book was written in 1994 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: -- observing the 1990 elections.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, I wonder if you can explain this for us. The winner of the election on the SDA was Mr. Abdic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The leading vote-getter for the presidency was Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Much more accurate than I posited; you're correct. Yet, as it turned out, Mr. Izetbegovic became the president of the presidency. How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: My last question on this area, sir, is you observe in your book, and I quote: "Many new leaders aroused fear and suspicion among the members of national minorities within their republics' boundaries." That's an observation you made in 1994 relative to those 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's an observation relative to the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and its various republics, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Now, very briefly, can we capsulise the different positions of the parties after the November 1990 elections relative to the future of Bosnia? The Serbian position was either a confederation or succession (sic)? Can we agree to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Malcolm, in his book, on page 223, is quoted as observing, quote, "By early 1991, Milosevic was saying publicly that if there were any attempt to replace the federal structure of Yugoslavia with some looser confederal arrangement, he would seek to annex whole areas of Bosnia and Croatia." Would you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I agree with that. I would disagree with your statement, which was not the same as what you just read.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And what part of my statement did you disagree with, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you like to repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, no, I don't, actually. Let's go on to the -- if we can see what the Croatian position was and if we have an agreement on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Stein, you said -- I think that is where the witness disagrees with you -- you said that there were several positions. (In English) You capsulised the different positions of the parties after the November 1990 elections relative to the future of Bosnia, the Serbian position was either confederation or succession. (Interpretation) This is what you asked. What do you mean by "succession"? (In English) I don't understand. What is -- succession to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let's try to break that question down. It was a poorly phrased question on my part. Do you agree that the Serbian position was -- let's just take one -- confederation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And what did you take that question to mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took it to mean that you didn't understand what Noel Malcolm wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. What was the Serbian position in 1991 relative to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As he said in the passage that you read, the Serb position, meaning that of Milosevic and the SDS, was either a centralised Yugoslavia, not a confederational Yugoslavia, but a centralised Yugoslavia or a secession of Serbian communities and the establishment of a greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let's take the second part of that question. The Croatian position, sir, was for a federation, fair enough?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HDZ position really changed over the course of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: November 1991 is a good time to pick because --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I want the Croatian position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there is no single Croatian position, as I've told you previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Then your answer is not important to me, sir. Now, let's move ahead --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm concerned about the witness not being allowed to answer questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask him in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm also concerned about quotations being put without the witness having documents to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see how we get on. I'm anxious to finish this examination. Yes, Mr. Stein?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I want to turn our attention, sir, to the response of the central government of BiH to the Serb aggression. You recognise, sir, do you not, that Mr. Izetbegovic declared in early October that Bosnia was neutral between Serbia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you specify the year, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I would say that was the position of the presidency, in the majority of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, we're making great progress, sir, so I want to turn your attention to one other thing, and that is, in the war itself, you make an observation in your book relative to the actual fighting and fighters on the ground. You noted that there were exclusively Muslim brigades, and this is a paraphrase, formed in the early days of the war to fight within the Bosnian army; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your research shows that there were, in fact, people from outside the region who came into Bosnia to fight this war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is different from the statement that you just read from my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me get directly to the statement from your book, and this is at page 267: "Fighting against Croatian units in Central Bosnia was done principally by Muslim brigades and Bosnian government forces and that region became almost exclusively Muslim." My question, sir, is where did these Muslim brigades come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A couple of different sources. First, when the mobilisation began at the time of the initial prospect of hostilities, the mobilisation was done on a territorial basis. There were a great many multi-ethnic units of the Territorial Defence force. Many of the Territorial Defence forces in Herzegovina were Muslim and Croat, many in Sarajevo were Muslim, Croat, and Serb, and as time went on, there tended to be a greater ethnic singularity to these units on all sides, first, because members who were not of the ethnic group often departed and sometimes they were expelled. So the first source is that there was this, I think, general process of the creation of ethnically more pure units that in some cases resulted in purely Muslim or purely Croat units. The second was specific brigades or units that were raised from early 1992 by leaders typically of the Territorial Defence or MUP, the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I want to specifically ask you whether these individuals you're referring to included individuals who called themselves Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, "Mujahedin" was a term that was frequently used by Croatian commentators as a pejorative term applying to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So at least through Croatian eyes, they were all Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I want to be very specific. Were there individuals fighting in the army of BiH who were from outside the region, that is to say, from Islamic countries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge, there were a very few.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So that means there were some?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Where did those people come from, from your research and study?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You mentioned in your book and in your testimony in Blaskic that the Muslim irregulars and gangs terrorised civilians in government-controlled areas during the spring of 1992. First, do you still agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Second, would you describe that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the statement speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Again, the book that you have on your desk, page 331, describes some of these forces. I'd like you to take a look at it. Now, we might have different editions, so let's make sure we have the right one before I point you to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope you bought this too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We bought several copies. We'll come back to it. I just wanted to ask you this about the -- we're looking at this edition. I don't know that it's the same as yours. It's on page 331.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me quote from it precisely. The 7th Muslim Brigade is the topic of the discussion. "This was explicitly Muslim rather than Bosnian in its origin. Its officers were hostile to Westerners, wore Islamic insignia, long beards, and greeted each other with the Arabic 'Selam Aleikum,' peace be with you. Their families attended Islamic education classes, and their wives and daughters increasingly wore veils in public." My first question to you, sir, is were you aware that there was a 7th Brigade operating in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Does the Silber book accurately describe them, based on your research and writings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: She goes on to note, next sentence, and then we'll put this book down: "For the first time, a strident xenophobic Muslim nationalism was being articulated in Bosnia. The politics of multi-ethnic tolerance, the officers of the 17th Muslim Brigade argued, had led to the destruction of the Muslim people. It was time for Muslims to take matters into their own hands, not as Bosnians but explicitly as Muslims." Agree or disagree with that observation of the Silber book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't agree in its totality, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sorry, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You do not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I want to set the stage here to where we're going on this ultimatum discussion. In order to do so, though, I think it's fair to discuss the refugees that were certainly disturbing the demographic structure in Bosnia. So let's start with this: We can agree, can't we, that in April of 1992 forward into 1993, major Bosnian cities were flooded with refugees.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I would actually date -- the date is much earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. What do you give us as the first date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started seeing refugees coming into Bosnia in significant numbers in the summer of 1991, during the war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: According to your book and your observations, and feel free to comment, less than three weeks after the EC recognised Bosnia's independence, the UNHCR estimated that 370.000 Bosnians had become refugees, by June 2nd, that number had reached 750.000, and by the fall of 1992, the Bosnian war had produced 2 million refugees, almost half of Bosnia's population, according to the 1991 census. Are those the numbers that you still, based on your current research, agree to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The numbers you are citing here are the total number of refugees created. They were not, by that time, anywhere near -- the majority of them were not in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: But about 1 million of them remain in Bosnia still; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you opined in your book, and I'm sure you'd still agree, that the refugees in Bosnia compounded the urgent needs of the civilians for food and basic supplies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let's go up to the spring of 1993. You've opined that there were, again, roughly a million refugees in Bosnia at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We may be saying the same thing, but I want to make sure we put this in context, the U.N. Commission on Human Rights reported, as of November 17, 1993, in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, there were over 2,1 million people displaced from their homes, nearly 50 per cent of the population recorded in the census of 1991. Now, that's for the totality of Yugoslavia; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You cited that it's the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, not Human Rights, but I otherwise concur with your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That work goes on to say that about 800.000 of the 2,1 million were estimated to have sought refuge outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina, while the rest were seeking refuge inside the country.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's, I think, fair to say that this was a process whereby typically when one became a refugee due to hostile action, one sought first refuge in a nearby town or city and, in many cases, ultimately moved outside of either Bosnia or the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And the million or 1,3 million, depending on the time and place, individuals in Bosnia who were refugees would sometimes move more than one time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They're still moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Of course. Now, with that in mind, with those numbers in mind, I'd ask you if your research can help us with this, relative to life from the ground up, if you will: During the war, the entire infrastructure of Bosnia-Herzegovina basically closed down; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not exactly. Actually, the infrastructure was seriously weakened before the war began and functioned at some minimal level, and its functioning during the war was highly dependent on the local circumstance. So there were places where I would say your statement is absolutely true --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and other places where things functioned at the same inadequate level they had functioned at before the war began.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And certainly services such as water, electrical, natural gas, oil, and the supplies of those necessities were diminished during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Municipal services, such as police, fire, ambulance, rescue, were all impacted by the lack of manpower and men being sent to the front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a general rule, those emergency services frequently worked better than some of the other more routine municipal services.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nevertheless, your observation is an accurate one, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. The currency was devalued and the monetary system collapsed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That pretty much happened before the war began.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And remained the same during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, the German mark became the currency well before the war began and remained the currency, at least in the areas controlled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In some cases, in the Croatian-controlled areas, the Croatian kuna became the currency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And state and federal services, such as health care, pensions, state programmes, disabilities, were delayed or impacted or diminished by the war as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The delay in pension payments preceded the war and continued to be in arrears throughout the war and continue, to this day, in almost all places to be substantially in arrears. So I don't know that the cause of that lateness or retardation can be judged to be the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The observation is correct, but the cause we separate on. All right. Schools were also affected by the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Shut down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most schools continued to function during the war to a surprising degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Their staffs were affected by people going to the front, obviously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Radio, TV, and newspapers were sporadic, at best?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's one area where the functioning continued, maybe even increased during wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: On all those medias?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In various places, depending on accessibility, as the well-known story of Oslobodenje in Sarajevo never missing a day of publication, and radio broadcasts were continued in many areas, and even, as I say, the stations in some instances increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: How about in the rural areas, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the media -- generally, the radio capabilities reached into the rural areas, in most cases, just fine. Newspapers were started in some small communities where none had existed before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. As I understand it as well, the gaols were opened up, that is to say, the gaols were closed down and the prisoners let out because they couldn't maintain the facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a very broad generalisation, and I wouldn't accept it for all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You certainly can accept that part of that statement is true. Gaols were opened in instances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what you're reading from, so I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do you know of any instance, sir, in which a prison or gaol was basically shut down and the prisoners released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You've heard of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was another consistent feature of, actually, life. There were periodic pardons that were executed by the presidency going back to the 1970s.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Sir, does your review also indicate that the courts within Bosnia-Herzegovina were closed or short-staffed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, many, many, I would say, not all, but that was an area that functioning was extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Factories were shut down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Shut down" is perhaps not the word. Many were already rendered idle by 1991 due to lack of supplies, the high cost of electricity, the difficulties getting adequate means for production, and many factories were bombed and destroyed during the war. So in general, the productive capability, from an industrial standpoint, with very few exceptions, shut down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And food supplies were limited; civilians had little to eat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, with some exceptions, that was true for much of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We can agree, can we not, that by the spring of 1993, inter-ethnic tensions were at an extremely high level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: These tensions and fears at times and in certain places were characterised by feelings such as terror, fear, and paranoia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We can agree, can we not, that in your opinion, the armed forces of all three sides had committed atrocities by the spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: This fact, in and of itself, furthered and increased tensions and volatility within Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, you claim that there was an ultimatum issued in April of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: April 3rd, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: As I understand it, the basis of your claim is newspaper accounts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The basis of my contention that this is an ultimatum is, first of all, the language of the alleged draft agreement between Mr. Boban and President Izetbegovic, the deadlines that are imposed within that agreement, the nature of the resolution that was passed by the HVO at its session on the 3rd of April, 1993, the response that the ultimatum evoked in various media, both within Croatia, the international media, and even Tanjug, the Serbian agency, and finally, the fact that the ultimatum was reiterated by the spokesman for the HVO at a press conference on the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And that spokesman would be who, in your opinion, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Vaso Vegar, I believe, is the name. Vaso Vegar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: First name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's V-O-S-O, if I have his name right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We're going to go through some of those in great detail, but let me start off by saying I would like you to have a look at another little exhibit we've made up, which we'd like to put on the ELMO and which we'd like to give to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which part of the evidence are you dealing with now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: This is the ultimatum issue, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The evidence in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The evidence in chief includes his expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whereabouts in the report is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I believe it's towards the back, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if you're going to cross-examine on it, you must refer us to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That would be roughly at pages 41, 42, 43, and 44. Now, sir, I started to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, wait a moment. I'm going to find it first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, which part of the report do you want to cross-examine on, Mr. Stein?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, I want to be very limited, sir, and that's going to be relative to page 43 in his conclusion that there was an ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Would you deal with it as expeditiously as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, are you done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Before April 15th, are you aware that there were a series of crimes against Croats in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were numerous conflicts, including civilian casualties, by both sides in Central Bosnia prior to April 3rd and prior to April 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me show you a chart prepared by us and see if we can agree that this represents some of the crimes against Croats in Central Bosnia in April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D45/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Before it's exhibited, we'll see whether the witness agrees with it or not. It may be, Mr. Stein, that you'll have to produce this by another route.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's fine, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just let the witness see it. Doctor, if you can agree with it, say so; but if you don't know or you feel you can't, also say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would feel I'm not qualified to judge the validity of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Hand it back to Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. We'll do it by other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: One of the witnesses in this case, sir, Mr. McLeod, testified on May 14th, at page 199 -- I'm sorry, at page 4 -- that the events in the middle of April leading up to the 16th, quote, "suggested there had been a long period of tension between the two ethnic groups in Central Bosnia. This appeared to have exploded on the morning of the 16th." That's consistent with your opinion of the tension level in Central Bosnia as of April 1993; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first sentence, I think, that you read, would be consistent with my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would take -- I wouldn't care to express it that way for the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Were you aware, sir, that on April 15, 1993, an HVO brigadier commander named Totic was kidnapped in Zenica and some of his bodyguards were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You were not aware of that at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do you know who Lieutenant-Colonel Robert Stewart is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: He was the BritBat commander for Central Bosnia during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart has opined in this courthouse, quote: "It is clear to me that the kidnapping of Totic --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, what's the point of this? The witness said that he is not aware of it, so there is no point putting something else about the kidnapping. You can put it to another witness or you can call evidence about it, but if a witness says that he is not aware of it, there's no point belabouring it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It's not that I want to belabour that point, sir; it's a different point. I'll try it in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your opinion is that the events of mid-April were as a result of threats issued in the media; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In essence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My statement, sir, is designed to address the political situation, and I have not opined on the tactical military unit operations either on the 16th of April or at any other time. I have simply noted that the HVO, which was in charge of the area at the time in kind of a martial-law capacity and was the head of the fused civil and military administration of the area, issued, in what appeared to be ambiguous terms, a specific ultimatum. It was interpreted as such at the time by a wide variety of observers in the region, both the local actors and outside observers. That's the essence of what I have put forward to you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It's the local actors of which I would like to speak. You haven't spoken with any of the local actors on the ground, have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. That is not something that I have addressed in this paper, nor would I claim to have spoken with them. It's beyond the scope of my direct testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And your answer, sir, to my question a few seconds ago was that your report was designed to address the political situation, and you have not opined on the tactical military unit operations either on the 16th of April or any other time. So if I take your answer, you're talking about a theory, but you have never spoken with the individuals on the ground --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, he's answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: By the way, sir, in your book, no mention is made of this ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Were you aware, also, sir, that the April 1993 agreement did in fact result in a joint command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot accept your characterisation of it as an agreement. It was never endorsed, signed by, or involved in any way the side of the ABH or the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The issue of a joint command was in fact a very old one, going back to early 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sir, let me just cut you off. You agree with part of my sentence but not all of it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't agree with any of it. As I heard you state, the agreement resulted in a joint command; I take exception to the use of the term "agreement."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And the term "joint command"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the fact that it led to or established a joint command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: If it please the Court, I would like to introduce, if I can, or maybe perhaps just read from -- would make it a lot faster -- a statement of Dzemo Merdan, who was the general of the HQ BiH army Sarajevo. He is quoted in his statement given to the Office of the Prosecution, quote: "On April 2nd, 1993, an agreement was signed between Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic that had a number of terms and conditions. The basis of this agreement was the work done by the joint commission, which I will refer to later. I was present at the negotiations that led to and followed that agreement. In the formal agreement, one of the terms was to the effect that units that had their origin from outside of the area in which they were present must leave within three days. This was particularly because HV soldiers were in the area, as evidenced by the one killed on a road between Vitez and Busovaca. Regarding the fourth term of that agreement, wherein it was decided that a joint command be formed between the HVO and the BiH, the joint command was formed at the end of April or the beginning of May 1993 with the HVO in Travnik, and it functioned for approximately 15 days, until the conflict in Travnik in May. The purpose of that term was to attempt to unite us against a common enemy, the Bosnian Serb army." Having read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Are you able to take this in, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I've followed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got the gist of it? Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: At least according to the general, there was an agreement and there was a joint command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe the general's story is correct. I think he has the date wrong. I think he has it about three weeks too early, and the date was the 3rd of August, not 2nd, and the track that President Izetbegovic followed was from Zagreb, on the 27th of March, back to Sarajevo, where on the 3rd of April, he presided over a meeting of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and met with the French ambassador. He was not in Mostar, which is the place at which the agreement was alleged to have been signed. He had no knowledge of this particular draft agreement. There were, however, subsequent talks, after the ceasefire that was arranged about -- in about the middle -- about the 22nd or 23rd of April, I believe, there was an effort by BritBat to bring about a ceasefire, and at that point, further discussions were held. So my best interpretation would be that he simply has the date wrong, and that makes his comments, if I'm correct about that, irrelevant to the ultimatum that we're discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: If you're correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Is this conclusion that you have, relative to this alleged ultimatum, something on which reasonable historians can reasonably disagree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My sense of it is that the evidence is very convincing and that there will always be people who will disagree with me on it, but I wouldn't accept your formulation that reasonable historians can reasonably disagree. I think reasonable historians would agree with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And some would not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some historians would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some attorneys might not either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I want to ask you, in conclusion, this: Colonel Stewart opines in his book that -- and I'll read it. Quote: "Bosnia is certainly complex beyond anyone's dreams. There are far more than three sides -- Serb, Croat and Muslim -- we hear about in the media. There are factions within groups and groups within factions, and without an established order, these different elements have created a situation as close to anarchy as I have witnessed." That's from Stewart's book. Have you read his book, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Is that a conclusion with which you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is applicable for various times and many places in Bosnia. I would say that his general characterisation makes even more unusual the ultimatum of April 3rd, because it was one of the few times in the war when the clear prevailing civil and military administration preannounced an intent to launch a military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: By the way, were you aware that Colonel Stewart also has told us that the HVO was totally unprepared for the events in the Lasva Valley on April 15th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, or Mr. Mikulicic? Mr. Mikulicic, how long are you going to be? It's five minutes to the break. Would you prefer to take the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it seems reasonable to take a break now, and then after that, I will need another half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. A quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good day, Dr. Donia. My name is Goran Mikulicic. I am an attorney from Zagreb, and in this case with my colleague, Kovacic, I represent Mario Cerkez, the second accused. I would like to ask you a few questions, so I would ask you to respond to them according to your best knowledge. Dr. Donia, before coming to the group of questions that I noted down, I would like to clarify two topics which, it seems to me, were not sufficiently explained in your testimony to date. The first topic that you mentioned recently, this afternoon, is when you said that the HVO, in the regions where it achieved its jurisdiction, introduced so-called martial law. Could you please explain what you meant when you said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I noted that it was a constitutionally provisioned martial law, and I'm referring to both the proclamation of July 3rd, 1992, which made the HVO the temporary supreme authority in the territory of Herceg-Bosna, and also the fusion of authority which took place, I believe, in November of 1992 in which the head of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and the HVO were fused in a single person. I use the term "martial law" as qualified by the rather unusual provisions that were included in the Act of July 3rd. My use of the term may, in fact, be unacceptable from the point of view of a constitutional perspective, I don't know, but it seems to me to aptly describe the situation as it prevailed in Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, what were the features of that rule that have inspired you to describe it as martial law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically, judicial functioning, including courts, and various administrative functions were consolidated under the leadership of a military organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, Judge Robinson, in a way, anticipated my next question, but I would be quite direct. Does that mean that, in your opinion, in those regions, all civil authority was suspended and substituted by military authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my interpretation, no, it was rather fused with military authority. I would note that in the objections of the members of the HDZ who opposed the formation of a stronger Herceg-Bosna, to them, and this was a proclamation issued on, I think, the 4th or 5th of July, 1993, the part that they objected to was not the existence of the HVO but that the HVO had now assumed administrative functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Dr. Donia, that the term "HVO" also included both the civilian and the military component?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar, Dr. Donia, with the fact that the military component of the HVO, in July 1992, was recognised as a legitimate component of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let's move to the second topic which I felt was not sufficiently clarified. This is the agreement that you cited between Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban, which was articulated by the spokesman Vaso Vegar. I would like to concentrate on point 2 of that agreement, so if you would permit me to read it as it's described here. That paragraph states: "All armed forces of the HVO and the police of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the police, the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which come from outside of the borders of the province, must be identified and leave those provinces within three days." Dr. Donia, could you please concentrate on the part that talks about the forces which come from outside of the province? What is your interpretation of this decree? Is this talking about all the forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the police or only those which happened to be in that region of the 8th, 9th, and 10th cantons but are not originally linked to those regions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I, first of all, cannot share your characterisation of this as an agreement because it was never discussed or entered into by President Izetbegovic. In fact, even the press coverage, which was written by the HVO spokesman, I believe, refers to it as a draft agreement and notes that it was yet to be signed by President Izetbegovic. I'm not in a position to interpret what the specific language of that article means. It, I think in some sense, was clear that there was to be a division of forces, but what was meant by the drafters in expressing the term "porijeklom" from origins outside the province, I don't know what that refers to. I'm not qualified to interpret it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donja, your report which we received regarding this topic concluded that the text that we have just read would mean, and I quote, "that all Bosnian forces must leave Provinces 3, 8, and 10 where they were present in a significant number." I could only interpret this statement of yours the way it was stated, "all forces," but this does not come out from this text, only those forces which are not originally from that region, and that is something different. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would, I guess, defer to what happened on the 16th of April, when actually at a press conference, Mr. Vegar clarified the terms of this ultimatum. At that press conference, he was asked whether the army of BiH and its units that were in Provinces 3, 8, and 10 had to lay down their arms. That was a question posed to him at the conference. His response was, "No. The requirement is either that the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina withdraw or submit themselves to HVO command."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, perhaps I'm insisting on this too much, but this is a very important fact, so I would like to ask for your understanding and also ask for the understanding of the Court. This is not in the form of an ultimatum, as you say, and that relates exclusively to the forces of the Bosnian army and the police, but also the Croatian army and the police in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which are not originally from the region of Provinces 3, 8, and 10 under the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the language refers to the withdrawal of the respective forces, not from Provinces 3, 8, and 10 but from the provinces in which they don't belong, that is, the notion would be that the forces of the HVO would, if there were any in those provinces, withdraw from provinces that were awarded to Bosnia-Herzegovina under Vance-Owen. Likewise, any troops that were army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or police units of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Provinces 3, 8, and 10 would be compelled to withdraw from those provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, if we accept your characterisation of this topic as an ultimatum, then is it true that the ultimatum was stated equally in relation to the HVO and the BH army? Because both units from these entities were supposed to withdraw from the provinces that they did not originally come from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The specific impact of the ultimatum depends on what units were where. If there were a host of ABiH units in Provinces 3, 8, and 10 and no HVO units in provinces awarded to Bosnia-Herzegovina, it would, indeed, be a unilateral ultimatum. If, on the other hand, there were forces of the HVO throughout the provinces of those awarded to the central government, it would not be a unilateral ultimatum and it would apply to all those forces. I don't know what specific units were deployed where at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Donia. We will move on to other topics. Yesterday, at the beginning of your testimony, my colleague Stein asked you if you had ever, while working on your report, spoken with Dario Kordic, did you ever ask to speak to him, and was it true that his name, the name of Dario Kordic, was not mentioned in your book from 1994. My question is, does this also apply to Mr. Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are two questions you're asking, and one is have I ever interviewed or met with your client, and the answer is no, I have not. The second question is does his name appear in the book, and the answer also is no, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I would like the usher to put document Z1660 on the ELMO, 1660. This is a map of the region of the former Yugoslavia that we are discussing, so in order to make the testimony more plastic, I would like to put a few questions to Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, we see a map of the region of the former Yugoslavia which is interesting to us only in order to establish or determine the borders of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in relation to the neighbouring republics, later states. Would you please point on the ELMO with which republics, that later became states, does -- which states border on Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two states border Bosnia-Herzegovina. One is the Republic of Croatia and the other is the reconstituted Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in its embodiment representing both the Montenegrin republic, the Serbian republic, and the Vojvodina, which was annexed to it in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, could you please just tell us briefly, which region did the main aggression against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina come from, and by that, I mean the aggression of the former Yugoslav People's Army and the paramilitary Serbian and Montenegrin units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aggression came from both the Republic of Croatia and the units of the Yugoslav National Army and Serbian paramilitary units. I respect your question and will identify it. The aggression came from the Montenegrin irregulars and paramilitaries who entered Herzegovina, it came from forces crossing the border with Serbia, and it came from within Bosnia-Herzegovina, including units of the JNA, numerous Serbian paramilitary units, and, in some cases, reconstituted Territorial Defence forces. Have I answered your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course. One explanation, when you mentioned that the aggression came partially from the territory of the Republic of Croatia, would you agree that by that, you mean parts of the Republic of Croatia which at that time were under the rule of Serbian paramilitary units and parts of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was indeed part of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Dr. Donia, that the border towards the southeast, towards Serbia and Montenegro, and then on the other side, in relation to the Republic of Croatia, in parts which were occupied by the JNA, were practically closed to citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? There was no border traffic across those borders; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you identify the time period that you're thinking of?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I mean the period from 1992 up until the Dayton Accord.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say, from the early summer of 1992, that that was a general statement one could make, yes. Probably also valid for some time after Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, Dr. Donia, the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina received humanitarian aid, received medicines, clothes; refugees were crossing the borders. Would you agree with me that this was border traffic that was exclusively conducted through the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Largely. There was substantial air assistance. I would note that my own entry into Bosnia and Herzegovina during wartime was always through Zagreb, and that in fact a great deal of humanitarian aid passed through the Republic of Croatia on the way to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Very frequently a substantial percentage of it was removed by forces of the Croatian army or HVO on the way in, but indeed, your basic point, I would concur that the border crossings into Bosnia and Herzegovina were largely through the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, would you agree with me that the Republic of Croatia, the next day after the declaration of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, recognised that state, and that it was the first state out of all the world's states which sent an ambassador to occupied Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Is this true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After a certain period of time, in Zagreb, the capital of the Republic of Croatia, an embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Dr. Donia, that throughout this whole period that we are talking about, from the moment when the embassies were established, the Croatian embassy in Sarajevo and the Bosnia and Herzegovinian one in Zagreb, that these embassies were continually active?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar, Dr. Donia, with the fact that at the Bosnian and Herzegovinian embassy in Zagreb in 1993, there was a military-economic representative office, as well as a logistical section of the headquarters of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as a sector of that headquarters in Split?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not aware of the Split office, but I was aware of the offices in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Permit me, Dr. Donia, to show you a document which I would like to introduce into evidence. I would like you to comment on it if you feel that this is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would the usher please ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D32/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you please be kind enough, Dr. Donia, to look at this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you agree if I say that this body operated on the 15th of July, 1993, in the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm really not qualified to, I guess, validate this document. I have no reason to doubt it and would find it in agreement with the general approach of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, but I really can't validate the document as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course. Dr. Donia, a moment ago, in answering questions by my colleague Mr. Stein, you touched on the question of refugees and their fate and their numbers as a consequence of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I should just like briefly to touch upon this topic. Would you agree with me, Dr. Donia -- and I have some figures here of the office for refugees and displaced persons of the government of the Republic of Croatia -- if I say that at the end of 1992, there were about 285.000 refugees from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that had found refuge in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that number is right. It accords with my understanding of the refugee reception by Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you know or did you come across in your research any data which would indicate that the government of the Republic of Croatia expelled refugees coming from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know of no such incident, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the course of your research, Mr. Donia, did you find any evidence of the Republic of Croatia during that time -- that is, end of 1992, 1993, and 1994 -- in any way confiscating the property of legal persons from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't answer that question. I have not made any point of investigating that question and couldn't really give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know, Dr. Donia, that the Republic of Croatia, in its hospitals, provided medical treatment to a large number of people coming from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina? And I particularly have in mind the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I'm not really familiar -- I would assume that there was medical care provided in refugee camps and in various facilities where refugees were housed and cared for by the UNHCR and other agencies, and that some of that came from the Republic of Croatia. But I must -- I'm reaching beyond my knowledge here to make that assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand that, Dr. Donia, but I hope you didn't misunderstand my question. I was not thinking of the refugee camps; I rather had in mind hospitals and regular medical facilities. In specific terms, do you know that the clinical hospital in Split, in the course of 1992 and 1993, hospitalised almost 4.000 persons of Muslim ethnicity from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know that number, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Dr. Donia, could you agree with me if I say that in 1992, 1993, and 1994, there were frequent meetings between statesmen or representatives of the state authorities of the Republics of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How would you describe those meetings, roughly? Were they frequent, or were they rare, infrequent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I really don't -- I think it varied from time to time, and in -- certainly in 1992, there were very regular, frequent contacts. I think they became somewhat less regular in the course of the spring and summer of 1993, but I think the contacts and meetings took place at many different levels, and it's difficult to characterise the frequency without looking at specific ministries or heads of state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Dr. Donia, are you aware that the Croatian parliament adopted a declaration with regard to the conflicts that occurred in Central Bosnia between the Croatian and Muslim sides, asking explicitly that those conflicts be halted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Dr. Donia, that the president of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, in April 1993 issued an appeal requesting that the conflicts in Central Bosnia be stopped between the Muslims and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, I should like to ask you to examine a document relating to this appeal of President Tudjman's and which I should like to tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher for his assistance to show this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D33/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you please focus on the last paragraph, which I should like you to examine more closely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you very briefly comment on those events and the meeting held in Zagreb on the 24th of April, 1993, under the auspices of Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I actually referred to it a few minutes ago in response to some of Mr. Stein's questions. In the wake of the violence on April 16th and that subsequent week, the international community actively promoted a ceasefire on the ground in Central Bosnia and rushed to move forward the arrangements of the Vance-Owen Plan. It will be remembered that Boban had signed this agreement already in January, and Izetbegovic had signed it already in March, with certain qualifications. So this document reflects the efforts to push the process forward by the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That document, among other things, refers to meetings between the two states, doesn't it? Between the presidents of the two states; I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it specifies -- the English language version I have says, "I welcome readiness expressed by the Croat and Muslim leaders in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic." It doesn't state between states, unless I'm directing my attention to a different section of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I think there must be a misunderstanding. My question was whether there was a meeting in Zagreb, attended by President Alija Izetbegovic, President Tudjman, and Lord Owen, which is referred to in this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't see a reference to a meeting with the three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, this appeal was made by Mr. Tudjman on the 22nd of April, 1993, and in the last sentence it says that it welcomes the readiness of the Croatian leaders and the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic, to meet with Lord Owen, and that meeting was attended by Lord Owen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if the meeting -- I assume the meeting took place, but I see no indication in this document that President Tudjman had attended a prior one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Dr. Donia, let us leave this matter aside, and let us turn to another area now which will also be the last area of my cross-examination. You have studied the history of the Balkans, and especially that of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Could you tell us, on the basis of those studies into distant history, how many wars were waged in that area, I do not mean the exact number, but how would you describe those wars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would certainly begin by noting that the two greatest wars of the 20th century on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina were major, bloody, large-scale confrontations, it took many, many casualties, those being World War II and the war of the 1990s -- wars of the 1990s. World War I, there was relatively little fighting on the territory of Bosnia. Prior to that, I would -- it's a very valid question, and I'm not sure how I would characterise it without thinking about it some more, but there were sporadic armed conflicts and occasional wars over some centuries, and they were of different types. There were territorial wars around the borders, some of which were no more than skirmishes, some of which were major battles. I would probably, just thinking back on the 19th century, consider the Austro-Hungarian invasion of 1878 to be perhaps the most substantial military action perhaps of that century.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, bearing in mind the wars between two states that occurred through history in this area, in your studies, did you ever come across an example of, during such war operations between two states, diplomatic relations between those two same states continuing uninterrupted? Have you ever come across a situation of that kind in your research?
