utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was typical of the earlier period anyway, for diplomatic relations to be maintained even as warfare went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: While states were at war, did ever one state service the other state with weapons, medicines, food, and other forms of aid, allowing it to pass through its territory? Have you ever come across such an example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that probably it was a very typical situation in earlier times for exactly that situation to prevail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, in your opinion, as a historian and a researcher of this issue, what is the reason, the cause of the conflict, of the war in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting. What I have in mind is the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims, to make it quite clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say, in a word, Karadjordjevo. It was the determination of the Croatian community, as it became transformed under the leadership of the Zagreb regime, to carve out a territory which would be dominated by the HVO and exclusively Croatian in character.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is your position, isn't it, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be my answer to your question, which was what was the primary cause of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, do you know somebody called Muhamed Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know him personally but I know who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell Their Honours the position this person had in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In October 1993, I believe he became foreign minister and was foreign minister until sometime around Dayton, and prior to that, I'm not certain what his function was, prior to October 1993. He was, for some time, the ambassador to the United Nations prior to becoming foreign minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Muhamed Sacirbey was the standing representative of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the United Nations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, is my conclusion correct, that the main function of an ambassador to the United Nations is to articulate the positions and policies of the state he represents in the International Community, that is, in the United Nations, to formulate the official positions of the state he represents? Would you agree with me in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be one of his functions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you to look at a document, with the help of the usher, written by Mr. Muhamed Sacirbey, standing representative to the United Nations, dated the 21st of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, the original version of this document is a bad one, so the Defence has copied it to facilitate reading, and I'm tendering both.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D34/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, will you please look at the second page? It is far more legible than the first. Would you please read this document, upon which I have a question for you or, rather, I will be asking you to comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: To fix this document in time, it is five days following the tragedy in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, is it true that Mr. Muhamed Sacirbey, and you agreed with me that his function is to articulate the official positions of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that he describes the conflict in Bosnia, and I'm drawing your attention to the fourth paragraph, as a conflict between local leaders which would never have occurred had it not been for the inadequate humanitarian aid given to the population of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I noted that one of his functions is to represent the official position of his government, and I note your reading of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Dr. Donia, thank you for answering my questions. The Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have several matters in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just dealing with that last document first, do you have any other comment to make on that passage in the statement of the United Nations, its validity or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would simply note its correspondence with the broad and longstanding objective of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina to lift the arms embargo, which is the principal purpose of this document. It is not designed to characterise the conflict but rather to seek assistance in the relief from the arms embargo of September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Going back to the earlier questions you were asked yesterday, first, dealing with questions directed, I think, to the integrity and so on of your report and other writings, when you started work on this region, did you have any personal historical sympathy to one side or the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any connection to any part of the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I've indicated in the personal statement, my entire family is American of Dutch extraction, and so I have no relationship, familial or origin, in any way connected to any part of Southeast Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked about your involvement under the National Peace Foundation. Is that a body that is partial in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the National Peace Foundation, except that it facilitated my visit in the summer of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked a number of questions about critics of your works. For convenience, there are collections of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If they are distributed in this way, as bundles, by the usher, first to the Court and to the witness, as they come, and then -- yes, exactly like that, to the Judges, to the witness, the Court, and the defendants. The documents have separate exhibit numbers. If you can give a bundle to the witness, please. Thank you. One bundle remains for the Court and one for each of the defendants. I've highlighted passages here for speed of finding and because they are the passages to which I'm taking the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First, the criticism by Kisslinger, not Kissinger, of September 12, 1994, does it deal with your book, A Tradition Betrayed, and highlighted in yellow in the first paragraph, you're described as "an expert on Islam under Hapsburg rule"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the bottom paragraph, "The unique Bosnian mix is, of course, well-known as a modern urban phenomenon ... but it is this book's particular accomplishment to trace it to the very advent of Bosnian Christianity and extend it to outlying towns and villages." Over the page, please, highlighted in red is the passage read to you by Mr. Stein. Its context was this. The first phrase or sentence even not read was: "Donia and Fine's view of Bosnian culture is on the whole compelling, but its presentation is troubling ..." The last paragraph reads as follows: "Still, like Vulliamy, Donia and Fine deepen our understanding of what has been lost in Bosnia, and underscore the distance between knowledge and political wisdom. Their efforts are valuable because the war in Bosnia has been fought to expunge its past while determining its fate. As a work that documents a legacy, Bosnia and Herzegovina: A Tradition Betrayed is an answer, however disproportionate, to the burning of the national archives in Sarajevo, the razing of hundreds of mosques and churches, the destruction of the Mostar, Bridge. What conquerors can blast from stone, they can never bottle the genie of historical memory." That was part, in any event, of the comments of Kisslinger on your work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is a French translation for that. But if we can turn swiftly to the next document, they've all been numbered, which should be 1677.3, this is a criticism by Legvold, and there was the one phrase put to you, "written with something of a skilled high-school text"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought that actually was pretty much the objective that we had in mind in writing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Shall we now look at the rest of the criticism? Because I'll tell you how that was characterised to you in a question. He suggested that this was not a very favourable criticism when that single line was put to you. Other passages read: "With the calm authority of their craft, they firmly crush the silliness of popular conception. Not only, they make plain, has Bosnia existed as a separate, identifiable entity over all these years with borders more intact than either Croatia or Serbia, but in terms of present century, it's never known ethnic conflict. This history, they insist, has through the centuries been one of tolerated diversity and practical compromise." The next paragraph before the single quoted phrase: "This book is only 270 pages of small-paged text, simply written, with something of the character of a skilled high-school text. That is appropriate. Given what the warring parties in the region are doing to their history, for others to be saving and preserving it for future generations is a modestly noble act." If we then turn to the next criticism by Fouad Ajami, three pages, dated August 7, 1995, is another comment on your book. The third sheet is a summary criticism of your work by -- do you know Ajami?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's at the Johns Hopkins Advanced School for International Studies, frequently a commentator as well for various television networks and, in my view, an outstanding scholar and analyst of, particularly, Islam and Middle Eastern countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the third sheet, the highlighted sentence reads: "In one of the best scholarly accounts and histories of the former Yugoslavia, Bosnia and Herzegovina: A Tradition Betrayed, historians Robert Donia and John Fine ..." and then goes off to summarise the book. Next sheet, please, 1677.5, a criticism by Abbas Milani. Known to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the publication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the San Francisco Chronicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Highlighted: "Bosnia and Hercegovina: A Tradition Betrayed brings a sober voice of academic scholarship into the discussion. Seeking to identify the traditions that have characterised Bosnian society through its history, Balkan historians John Fine and Robert Donia explore the historical roots of Bosnian society from the arrival of Slavic tribes in the sixth and seventh centuries to the breakup of socialist Yugoslavia." Over the page, highlighted: "The authors try to steer a fair and dispassionate course." They praise your prose and they conclude at the end: "Erudite and impartial, 'Bosnia and Hercegovina: A Tradition Betrayed' greatly illuminates the rich contours of Bosnian history and the genealogy of its current tragic predicament." I think the next and perhaps last is a document numbered 1677.6, again by Fouad Ajami dealing with a number of books. I think on the third sheet, there's one sentence highlighted in red but the balance in yellow, where he's dealing with: "This history is an invention, spun out of vanity and a need for consolation." He goes on: "For fate meandered in the Balkans. And its meanderings can now be more clearly understood, and measured against some of the region's deadly myths, thanks to the appearance of outstanding works of research by the impassioned British journalist Noel Malcolm, the exacting American historians Robert Donja and John Fine ..." and he then goes on to deal with others, and he's praise-worthy of your work, three sheets or two sheets further on, in a passage highlighted, again, in yellow. The last document I'll deal with in a minute. Are those the criticisms that were being made of your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the people who made them, apart from one of whom you were unaware, peers, superiors, how would you categorise them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In many cases, peers; in some cases, people who have been longer than I have in the business of studying the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While we have the exhibits with us, and it's a small point that can be dealt with very swiftly, you were asked about the representation in countries other than the region of the party of the Bosnian Muslims. Are you aware of the representation in other countries around the world at that same time of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was actually something that all three parties engaged in at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that if you just look at the last exhibit that was at the bottom of the pile of documents, tell us what the document is, if you can?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Glaska Hrvatska Demokratska (phoen). It's "Merry Christmas and Happy 1990."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What is the document itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the journal of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we turn over and just look at the highlighted pages, we see references to, first, North America, I think. Following some pages with pictures, we see Australia, Sweden, and reports from associated groups elsewhere in the world?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Australia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked about President Tudjman, his revision of a text because of its having caused ethnic offence. Are you aware of any other examples of President Tudjman causing ethnic offence? Are you aware of a television programme where he spoke of his wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. And any other examples of his causing offence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The term "Bosniak," you've defined its present use. Did it, in fact, have an earlier use, however slight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It had many earlier uses, and there are many instances of earlier usage. The Bosniak historians have made a point of identifying these instances. As I look at them, the same problem occurred historically that occurs today, which is that at times, the term "Bosniak" applies to clearly the Bosnian Muslims, and at times, it's ambiguous whether it applies to the Muslims or to the inhabitants of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But there are historical precedents in which people call them Bosniaks and others call them Bosniaks as well, and those are situations in which the people concerned are Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked about a number of meetings of leaders, including, of course, Karadjordjevo. Is there a meeting at Grac and is there a meeting at Tikvis that you can help us with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The follow-up to the meeting in Karadjordjevo, in which the two heads of state conferred regarding the division of Bosnia, was followed on May 6th, 1992 by a meeting between Mate Boban and Radovan Karadzic in Grac which produced an agreement. It was a publicly released agreement that referenced the 1939 banovina line and agreed to work together further regarding a dual party cooperation. This was subsequently followed by, really, several other meetings in which, in June, President Tudjman met with first the Herzegovinian Croats on June 13th and then June 20th with the Bosnian Croats, and further, the implementation, albeit a delayed implementation, of this politics of division.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tikvis? No? Very well. You were asked many questions about efforts to create a Muslim state. Are you aware, yourself, of any efforts, in particular of any documents reflecting efforts to Catholicise areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina with which we are concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Catholicise areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By which I mean moves to encourage the erection of religious symbols of the Catholic faith, and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I interpreted your question to mean Catholic proselytisation or -- establish a more Catholic state, and I would say that there were some efforts to support the formation and strengthen Herceg-Bosna by certain clergy, and there was a great deal of support for the establishment of Catholic churches, support for the clergy, and so on, as a part of the broad effort, to, say, strengthen Croatian culture and religion. Actually, the majority of the leaders of the Franciscan order of Srebrna Bosna and the Catholic hierarchy, which to this day is in Sarajevo, was quite bitter about the formation of a purely territorial unit, and on at least some occasions strongly denounced such a solution, which left, in their view, these hundreds of thousands of Croat Catholics out of the community which had been proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When asked about the involvement of outsiders on the side of the Bosnian Muslims, were there outsiders involved in the HV or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at many different times. I think it's worth recalling that on May 15th, 1992, the Security Council passed a resolution which called for the withdrawal of foreign troops from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including those of the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Croatia, and so clearly at that time, in the view of the United Nations Security Council, there were outsiders -- namely Croatian forces and Serbian forces -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were also various -- the same resolution called for all paramilitaries to be brought under the command, the central command, of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or I think it's -- the language is it's under the command of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you were asked about Mujahedin, was it the case that there were individuals, whether mercenaries or otherwise, involved in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were mercenaries -- there were volunteers from Croatian communities around the world. There were mercenaries from a number of different countries, European countries and countries of the former Soviet bloc, that were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were stopped from giving your position on the Croatian position in November 1991 because you didn't agree with either of the two alternatives put to you. What do you say that position was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Croatian position at that time was in transition, and there was no single Croatian position but rather the first emergence of two different ones. The position of the elected leader of the HDZ in the elections of 1990, Stjepan Kljujic, was that the Croatian nation should support a unified Bosnia and Herzegovina and realise its national aspirations within the framework of that republic. The situation at the time was at the very end of the war in Croatia, and consequently that support was frequently conditional on the understanding that Bosnia and Herzegovina would eventually break away from, rather than remain part of, Yugoslavia. Thus, at this time, the second viewpoint emerged, which was that there should be a partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, either outright or in the form of the canton formula that the international community promoted. I've noted in my paper the two very different responses to the formation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna by Mate Boban, who saw it as a realisation of a territorial aspiration from the 1939 banovina boundary, and that of Mr. Kljujic, who saw this as a reluctantly-taken step that would not be implemented at this time. So subsequently, of course, with the expulsion and purging of the party at the direction of the Zagreb regime, Mr. Kljujic resigned as president and was subsequently replaced, and the party then adopted at that time the position that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, with its territorial designation, was the realisation of Croatian aspirations in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel Stewart's book, which you've read, do you have any observations to make on his commentary generally or on his observations of historical matters, he being an officer who was there for six months, I believe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think he has a -- his reportage on contemporary events is certainly worthy of note and important. His understanding of history or his relation -- his imparting of history I think is somewhat superficial, if you will, and I don't think he was intending to be a purveyor of serious history in that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The creation of mutual embassies by Croatia and by Bosnia-Herzegovina; any significance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I think that's a very important part of this two-track policy that the Zagreb regime maintained toward Bosnia at this time, and numerous observers have commented on this prolific production of statements, guarantees, appeals, by President Tudjman and various members of the Zagreb regime, recognising borders, recognising the legitimacy of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and at the same time the support, which was also really overt, of the separatist territorial aspirations of Croats in Bosnia. This really came to a head, I think, in the July 3rd, 1992, proclamation which was read in the world press as a stab in the back to Bosnia. The government -- or the official Russian agency, Itar Tass, simply stated that the Zagreb government is now pursuing the same policy as the Belgrade government. So this policy of supporting the separatist territorial ambitions of the Bosnian Croats coincided in time and at all times ran parallel to this other track, which was a plethora of pronouncements, recognition, exchange of ambassadors, and at all times things that were viewed as required by the international community in terms of the posture towards Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your judgement, were those other actions on the second track truly sincere or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think they were both real tracks, but it seems to me it's hard to view the expressions of support for the territorial integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina as sincere when Croatian forces were in Bosnia and Herzegovina and a separatist agenda was being promoted. So I would not view them as sincere, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've referred to two meetings of June the 13th and June 20th; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which year? Just for clarification; there may be a problem on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those meetings occurred in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. You started this afternoon by correcting certain matters that had been put to you in a selective way from the Silber & Little book. You also drew to the Court's attention that Kordic was referred to in that book, at least in the later edition of it. Is there anything you want to add to about that, and to what does it go?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the examination was stopped at that point. If we're to have quotations of that sort from the book, then we need the authors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got very much more? We're past our time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, if you can give me just a couple of minutes, I can certainly conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a matter of a quick point of history, kuna, the currency you referred to, where was that derived as a name, and was it controversial or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The kuna is a small animal, the skins of which were used, supposedly, at the time of the medieval Croatian kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had the name been used earlier as a currency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was also a reference to currency used in World War II by the Ustasha independent state of Croatia. Its adoption, I think in 1993, was very controversial and was viewed as a nationalist symbolic assertion by the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked questions about the media, and the newspapers in particular. The newspapers, did they survive the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, local newspapers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those that did, what was their content, in your judgement, as to its genuine political commentary or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, well, there were all sorts of publications, and the classic example, perhaps, is Oslobodjenje, the Sarajevo paper, which indeed came out I think every day except one when the printing ink froze. But there were many local publications, some of which had very tendentious agendas and others of which were pretty good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I think probably I'm going to leave that there, and the only other thing I have is a correction which I think I want to -- yes, one last question: The 17th (sic) Muslim Brigade, there was something that -- you were, I think, unhappy with the way the question was put to you about that. Is there anything you want to add? If you can't remember, it doesn't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 7th Muslim brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's too complicated to ask you all to go back to the relevant passage, but can I here note that at page 18 of today's transcript, line 5, Mr. Stein, in reading an extract from your book, Dr. Donia, on page 267, read it incorrectly, and it probably should be corrected for fear of otherwise being accidentally misleading. It was suggested, I think, that -- it was read in this way, or something to this effect: "Fighting against Croatian units in Central Bosnia was done principally by Muslim brigades," and then I think it says, "became exclusively Muslim." What your book said was, "And the Bosnian government forces in that region became almost exclusively Muslim."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It wasn't referring to the area becoming exclusively Muslim or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is a small correction to Merdan's statement, but I don't think it's significant. That's all I have to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Doctor, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got the next witness to call tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That will take an hour or so; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In chief, I would have thought I will be between three-quarters of an hour and an hour, but I hope not more. It could be less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The film has been seen now by one member of the bench and will be seen by the other tomorrow before the sitting, although I gather Mr. Stein has a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. We would object -- Your Honour's seen the film, so you know thoroughly, we find, frankly, its relevance attenuated. It is not part of the expert's report, nor does he say that he has relied on it. I'm not sure why it's being incorporated through his testimony at all. It is of an unnamed Muslim family and an unstated date. We have no access to the author of the film, although I gather her name is Tone Bringa. She is not on the witness list; she is the narrator. We have no access, either, to Debbie Christie, the producer or director, and I'm not sure how I would even begin to approach it. Now, I will concede, frankly, that it is, in my view, not particularly relevant except to prejudice the Court, and of course you are professional judges, and I'm not going to think for one minute that it will prejudice your judgement. But when you see the whole thing, as Your Honour has, it's a sad tale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to add only one sentence. We think that having that reader as part of Dr. Allcock's testimony is not appropriate. It is not because the discovery was not done appropriately, since we all voted yesterday, and indeed, only twelve hours before. I don't oppose, as a principle matter, a possibility for the Prosecution to enter that film in any other way or any other method throughout his case, but not connected to Dr. Allcock's testimony, since he never mentioned that movie.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just deal with the position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When Dr. Allcock arrived some days ago, he volunteered that film as a piece of effective field research that he would like to refer to in support of his conclusions. It was not known to him that the film happened to have been seen in another case by the author of the film a week before, and it was just a coincidence. He regards it as a piece of research upon which he would rely, much like any other piece of research. The position is now clear that his cross-examination will not be concluded, I think, tomorrow, and he will have to come back. And it can't be next week; it will have to be at some later date, probably I think now in September, but it may be an earlier date. It's possible. It certainly can't be next week; I think he is examining some doctoral candidates or something to that effect. Therefore the film will not prejudice the defendants because they will always be in a position to deal with it by cross-examination at a later day. As to calling the author of that film, she is not on the witness list, and indeed, I wasn't aware of her potential to assist us until, by the independent route, I had heard of her appearing in the other case a week ago. I gather there had been problems, in any event, with her attendance as a witness, and she was called by the Court, not by one of the parties, in the other case. Of course, if it's appropriate for her to be called and to ask questions, we can do that. Equally, it may be cross-examination in the other court would be relied upon, if that would assist. But the document itself is a piece of original research and is something that the witness may very well refer to in any event. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll decide about this tomorrow. Meanwhile, we will have all looked at the film by tomorrow, and we'll let you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Half past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 5.50 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of July, 1999, at 2.30 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
